questions.q: Tyler has read a tutorial three times, yet he still can't remember it when he needs it at work. Which change would help him most?
questions.hint: Which activity makes the brain work hardest?

options.text: Reading it a fourth time, more carefully
options.why: Re-reading makes it feel familiar, but the brain never has to work, so the memory stays weak.

options.text: Closing the tutorial and trying to recall it on his own
options.why: The effort of remembering (active recall) is what makes a memory strong.

options.text: Copying the whole thing word for word into a notebook
options.why: Copying is just reading once more. He is still not recalling anything by himself.

options.text: Finding a longer tutorial
options.why: The problem is not a lack of information. It is a lack of review.

questions.q: Which of these genuinely help you remember?
questions.hint: All but one of them work. Which one gives the brain no time to settle?

options.text: Reviewing every few days
options.why: Reviewing with gaps (spaced repetition) slows down forgetting.

options.text: Thinking of the answer before looking at it
options.why: This is active recall, the most powerful learning technique there is.

options.text: Finishing a whole topic in one night
options.why: Cram it all in one sitting and most of it is gone the next day; the brain gets no time to organize it.

options.text: Looking at pictures and text together
options.why: The idea gets stored two ways (dual coding), so you have two routes back to it.

questions.q: You got a quiz question wrong. What is the best thing to do next?
questions.hint: If you never find out why you got it wrong, you will make the same mistake again.

options.text: Read the explanation on the right and open the slide it links to
options.why: An explanation that arrives right after a mistake is the one you remember best.

options.text: Move on to the next question quickly
options.why: Moving on without knowing why leaves the wrong idea in your head.

options.text: Feel bad and close the quiz
options.why: Getting things wrong is the whole point of a quiz: it shows you where the gaps are.

questions.q: How much should you study in one sitting to learn best?
questions.hint: Small pieces are easier to remember.

options.text: One sub-segment: 10 to 15 minutes
options.why: The brain can easily organize a small piece, and you don't get tired.

options.text: A whole topic, from start to finish
options.why: When that much comes in at once, the new pieces push the earlier ones out.

options.text: Until you feel sleepy
options.why: A tired brain stores nothing; you are just spending time.

questions.q: Why is the answer hidden in the "Ask yourself" box under each slide?
questions.hint: If the answer were right in front of you, would you think for yourself?

options.text: So that you try to recall it yourself first
options.why: Thinking before you look is active recall. With the answer visible, your eyes would jump straight to it.

options.text: To save space on the page
options.why: Space is not the issue. It is a learning technique, not a design limitation.

options.text: Because the answer is not important
options.why: The opposite: it is the most important part of the slide, which is why you are asked to work it out yourself.

questions.q: Where is the problem in the code below?
questions.hint: If two customers enter this code in the same millisecond, what stock value does each one see?

options.text: When two requests arrive together, both see stock > 0, so more gets sold than exists
options.why: Checking and decrementing are separate steps, and in the gap a second request sees the old stock.

options.text: flush() should have been called twice
options.why: No matter how often you call flush(), two requests can still read the old value together.

options.text: find() is slow; findOneBy() should be used
options.why: Speed isn't the problem here; the gap between the two steps is.

options.text: There's no problem — it works fine when tested alone
options.why: Alone, requests arrive one after another, so this trap is never caught that way.

questions.q: Two customers buy the last phone at the same instant. Which stock update is safe?
questions.hint: Where does the "is any left?" check happen: in PHP, or inside the statement the database runs?

options.text: UPDATE product SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = :id AND stock > 0, then check the rows changed
options.why: The check and the change are one step. The second customer matches 0 rows and is told "sold out".

options.text: Read the stock, check it is above 0 in PHP, then UPDATE product SET stock = :newStock
options.why: Same gap as before: both customers read 1, both write 0, and two phones are sold.

options.text: UPDATE product SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = :id, with no condition
options.why: The decrement is safe but nothing stops it going below 0, so stock drops to -1 and a phone that doesn't exist is "sold".

options.text: Re-read the stock just before flush()
options.why: That only makes the gap shorter. Two requests can still slip through it.

questions.q: Which of these are architectural decisions?
questions.hint: Which ones would take weeks or months to change six months from now?

options.text: Which database to use
options.why: Switching databases in a system full of data is a huge, risky job.

options.text: Where to split the services
options.why: If the boundaries are wrong, you have to re-split the code, the data and the teams — all three.

options.text: The name of a private method
options.why: It changes in a minute and nobody else's code breaks.

options.text: The shape of a public API response
options.why: Mobile apps and partners depend on it; changing it breaks everything of theirs.

questions.q: What is the best question for deciding how much time a decision deserves?
questions.hint: Think of the difference between wall paint and a pillar.

options.text: How much will it cost to change this later?
options.why: The cost of changing it tells you whether the decision is paint or a pillar.

options.text: Is this the newest technology?
options.why: New doesn't mean better; new technology brings more unknown problems.

options.text: What do the big companies use?
options.why: Their problems aren't yours; their solution can be extra weight for you.

options.text: Which option needs the fewest lines of code?
options.why: Fewer lines doesn't mean the right decision; what matters is the consequences.

questions.q: On Black Friday night, 35 orders came in for 20 phones. What kind of problem is this?
questions.hint: Many people pressed "Buy" at the same instant.

options.text: A race condition — simultaneous requests decided based on stale stock
options.why: Each request saw stock available, then decremented it separately, so the numbers didn't add up.

options.text: The server was short of RAM
options.why: Low RAM makes a site slow or down; it doesn't cause wrong sales numbers.

options.text: The database was too slow
options.why: Slowness means longer waits; the wrong count comes from the gap between the two steps.

options.text: The button in the Vue app had a bug
options.why: Each customer pressed once; the problem is in the server's bookkeeping.

questions.q: After "Place order", sending the email takes 4 seconds and the user just waits. What is the best fix?
questions.hint: Does the email really have to arrive this very instant?

options.text: Hand the email job to a queue and respond immediately
options.why: The order is confirmed at once, and a worker sends the email in the background.

options.text: Buy a more powerful server
options.why: The delay is waiting for the email service to answer; no server, however strong, shortens that.

options.text: Stop sending the email
options.why: The customer needs the email; the job isn't dropped, just done later.

options.text: Show a loading spinner
options.why: A spinner makes the wait prettier, not shorter.
